sp.p: He says praesto , sir: whensoever your worship needs him, he can be ready with the like. He got this cold with sitting up late and singing catches with cloth-workers.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No more. I thank him.

sp.speaker: PARSON
sp.p: He coughs. God keep your worship and give you much joy with your fair spouse. Umn, uhm.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, Oh! Stay Cutbeard! Let him give me five shillings of my money back. As it is bounty to reward benefits, so is it equity to mulct injuries. I will have it. What says he?

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: He cannot change it, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: It must be changed.

p.seg: Cough again.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What says he?

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: He will cough out the rest, sir.

sp.speaker: PARSON
sp.p: [Coughs] again. Umh, umh, umh.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Away, away with him, stop his mouth; away, I forgive it−

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Fie, Master Morose, that you will use this violence to a man of the church.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: It does not become your gravity or breeding (as you pretend in court) to have offered this outrage on a waterman, or any more boist’rous creature, much less on a man of his civil coat.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: You can speak then!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Yes, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Speak out, I mean.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Ay, sir. Why, did you think you had married a statue? or a motion only? one of the French puppets with the eyes turned with a wire? or some innocent out of the hospital, that would stand with her hands thus, and a plaice-mouth, and look upon you?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh immodesty! A manifest woman! What, Cutbeard!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Nay, never quarrel with Cutbeard, sir, it is too late now. I confess it doth bate somewhat of the modesty I had, when I writ simply maid; but I hope I shall make it a stock still competent to the estate and dignity of your wife.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: She can talk!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Yes, indeed, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What sirrah! None of my knaves there? [Enter MUTE.] Where is this impostor, Cutbeard?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Speak to him, fellow, speak to him. I’ll have none of this coacted, unnatural dumbness in my house, in a family where I govern.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: She is my regent already! I have married a Penthesilea, a Semiramis, sold my liberty to a distaff!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Where’s Master Morose?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Is he come again? Lord have mercy upon me!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I wish you all joy, Mistress Epicene, with your grave and honourable match.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: I return you the thanks, Master Truewit, so friendly a wish deserves.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: She has acquaintance too!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: God save you, sir, and give you all contentment in your fair choice here. Before I was the bird of night to you, the owl, but now I am the messenger of peace, a dove, and bring you the glad wishes of many friends to the celebration of this good hour.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What hour, sir?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Your marriage hour, sir. I commend your resolution, that (notwithstanding all the dangers I laid afore you, in the voice of a night-crow) would yet go on, and be yourself. It shows you are a man constant to your own ends, and upright to your purposes, that would not be put off with left-handed cries.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: How should you arrive at the knowledge of so much?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, did you ever hope, sir, committing the secrecy of it to a barber, that less then the whole town should know it? You might as well ha’told it the conduit, or the bakehouse, or the infantry that follow the court, and with more security. Could your gravity forget so old and noted a remnant as lippis et tonsoribus notum ? Well, sir, forgive it yourself now, the fault, and be communicable with your friends. Here will be three or four fashionable ladies from the college to visit you presently, and their train of minions and followers.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Bar my doors! Bar my doors! Where are all my eaters, my mouths now? [Enter SERVANTS.] Bar up my doors, you varlets!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: He is a varlet that stirs to such an office. Let ’em stand open. I would see him that dares move his eyes toward it. Shall I have a barricado made against my friends, to be barred of any pleasure they can bring in to me with their honourable visitation?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: O Amazonian impudence!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, faith, in this, sir, she speaks but reason, and methinks is more continent than you. Would you go to bed so presently, sir, afore noon? A man of your head and hair should owe more to that reverend ceremony, and not mount the marriage-bed like a town bull or a mountain goat; but stay the due season, and ascend it then with religion and fear. Those delights are to be steeped in the humour and silence of the night; and give the day to other open pleasures and jollities of feasting, of music, of revels, of discourse: we’ll have all, sir, that may make your hymen high and happy.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, my torment, my torment!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, if you endure the first half hour, sir, so tediously, and with this irksomness, what comfort or hope can this fair gentlewoman make to herself hereafter, in the consideration of so many years as are to come−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Of my affliction. Good sir, depart and let her do it alone.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I have done, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: That cursed barber!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: (Yes, faith, a cursed wretch indeed, sir.)

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I have married his cittern, that’s common to all men. Some plague above the plague−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: (All Egypt’s ten plagues−)

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Revenge me on him.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: ’Tis very well, sir. If you laid on a curse or two more, I’ll assure you he’ll bear ’em. As, that he may get the pox with seeking to cure it, sir? Or, that while he is curling another man’s hair, his own may drop off? Or, for burning some male bawd’s lock, he may have his brain beat out with the curling-iron?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No, let the wretch live wretched. May he get the itch, and his shop so lousy as no man dare come at him, nor he come at no man.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: (Ay, and if he would swallow all his balls for pills, let not them purge him.)

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Let his warming-pan be ever cold.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: (A perpetual frost underneath it, sir.)

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Let him never hope to see fire again.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: (But in hell, sir.)

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: His chairs be always empty, his scissors rust, and his combs mould in their cases.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Very dreadful that! (And may he lose the invention, sir, of carving lanterns in paper.)

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Let there be no bawd carted that year to employ a basin of his, but let him be glad to eat his sponge for bread.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And drink lotium to it, and much good do him.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Or for want of bread−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Eat ear-wax, sir. I’ll help you. Or, draw his own teeth and add them to the lute-string.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No, beat the old ones to powder and make bread of them.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, make meal o’the millstones.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: May all the botches and burns that he has cured on others break out upon him.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And he now forget the cure of ’em in himself, sir; or, if he do remember it, let him ha’ scraped all his linen into lint for’t, and have not a rag left him to set up with.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Let him never set up again, but have the gout in his hands for ever. Now no more, sir.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, that last was too high set! You might go less with him, i’faith, and be revenged enough; as, that he be never able to new-paint his pole−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Good sir, no more, I forgot myself.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Or, want credit to take up with a comb-maker−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No more, sir.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Or, having broken his glass in a former despair, fall now into a much greater, of ever getting another−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I beseech you, no more.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Or, that he never be trusted with trimming of any but chimney-sweepers−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Sir−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Or, may he cut a collier’s throat with his razor by chance-medley, and yet be hanged for’t.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I will forgive him, rather than hear any more. I beseech you, sir.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: This way, madam.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, the sea breaks in upon me! Another flood! An inundation! I shall be o’erwhelmed with noise. It beats already at my shores. I feel an earthquake in myself for’t.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: [Kissing Epicene] ’Give you joy, mistress.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Has she servants too?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I have brought some ladies here to see and know you. She kisses them severally as he presents them. My lady Haughty, this my lady Centaure, Mistress Dol Mavis, Mistress Trusty, my lady Haughty’s woman. Where’s your husband? Let’s see him: can he endure no noise? Let me come to him.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What nomenclator is this?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Sir John Daw, sir, your wife’s servant, this.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: A Daw, and her servant! O, ’tis decreed, ’tis decreed of me, and she have such servants.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay sir, you must kiss the ladies, you must not go away now; they come toward you to seek you out.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: I’faith, Master Morose, would you steal a marriage thus, in the midst of so many friends, and not acquaint us? Well, I’ll kiss you, notwithstanding the justice of my quarrel. You shall give me leave, mistress, to use a becoming familiarity with your husband.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Your ladyship does me an honour in it, to let me know he is so worthy your favour; as you have done both him and me grace, to visit so unprepared a pair to entertain you.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Compliment! Compliment!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: But I must lay the burden of that upon my servant here.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: It shall not need, Mistress Morose; we will all bear, rather than one shall be oppressed.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I know it, and you will teach her the faculty, if she be to learn it.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Is this the silent woman?

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Nay, she has found her tongue since she was married, Master Truewit says.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Oh, Master Truewit! ’Save you. What kind of creature is your bride here? She speaks, methinks!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, madam, believe it, she is a gentlewoman of very absolute behavior and of a good race.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: And Jack Daw told us she could not speak!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: So it was carried in plot, madam, to put her upon this old fellow, by Sir Dauphine, his nephew, and one or two more of us; but she is a woman of an excellent assurance, and an extraordinary happy wit and tongue. You shall see her make rare sport with Daw ere night.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: And he brought us to laugh at her!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: That falls out often, madam, that he that thinks himself the master-wit is the master-fool. I assure your ladyship, ye cannot laugh at her.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: No, we’ll have her to the college: and she have wit, she shall be one of us! Shall she not, Centaure? We’ll make her a Collegiate.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Yes, faith, madam, and Mavis and she will set up a side.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Believe it, madam, and Mistress Mavis, she will sustain her part.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: I’ll tell you that when I have talked with her and tried her.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Use her very civilly, Mavis.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: So I will, madam.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Blessed minute, that they would whisper thus ever.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: In the meantime, madam, would but your ladyship help to vex him a little: you know his disease, talk to him about the wedding-ceremonies, or call for your gloves, or−

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Let me alone. Centaure, help me. Master bridegroom, where are you?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, it was too miraculously good to last!

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: We see no ensigns of a wedding here, no character of a bridal: where be our scarves and our gloves? I pray you give ’em us. Let’s know your bride’s colours and yours at least.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Alas, madam, he has provided none.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Had I known your ladyship’s painter, I would.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: He has given it you, Centaure, i’faith. But do you hear, Master Morose, a jest will not absolve you in this manner. You that have sucked the milk of the court, and from thence have been brought up to the very strong meats and wine of it, been a courtier from the biggin to the nightcap (as we may say), and you to offend in such a high point of ceremony as this, and let your nuptials want all marks of solemnity! How much plate have you lost today (if you had but regarded your profit,) what gifts, what friends, through your mere rusticity?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Madam−

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Pardon me, sir, I must insinuate your errors to you. No gloves? No garters? No scarves? No epithalamium ? No masque?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Yes, madam, I’ll make an epithalamium , I promise my mistress; I have begun it already: will you ladyship hear it?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Ay, good Jack Daw.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Will it please your ladyship command a chamber and be private with your friend? You shall have your choice of rooms to retire to after; my whole house is yours. I know it hath been your ladyship’s errand into the city at other times, however now you have been unhappily diverted upon me; but I shall be loath to break any honourable custom of your ladyship’s. And therefore, good madam−

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Come, you are a rude bridegroom, to entertain ladies of honour in this fashion.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: He is a rude groom indeed.

p.seg: Do not mistake me, sir; I but speak this to give the ladies some heart again, not for any malice to you.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Is this your bravo , ladies?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: As God help me, if you utter such another word, I’ll take mistress bride in and begin to you in a very sad cup, do you see? Go to, know your friends and such as love you.

div2.head: ACT 3 SCENE 7

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: By your leave, ladies. Do you want any music? I have brought you variety of noises. Play, sirs, all of you.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, a plot, a plot, a plot, a plot upon me! This day I shall be their anvil to work on, they will grate me asunder. ’Tis worse than the noise of a saw.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: No, they are hair, rosin, and guts. I can give you the receipt.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Peace, boys!

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Play, I say.

p.seg: You see who’s your friend now, sir? Take courage, put on a martyr’s resolution. Mock down all their attemptings with patience. ’Tis but a day, and I would suffer heroically. Should an ass exceed me in fortitude? No. You betray your infirmity with your hanging dull ears, and make them insult: bear up bravely and constantly. Look you here, sir, what honour is done you unexpected by your nephew: a wedding-dinner come, and a knight-sewer before it, for the more reputation; and fine Mistress Otter, your neighbour, in the rump or tail of it.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Is that Gorgon, that Medusa come? Hide me, hide me!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I warrant you, sir, she will not transform you. Look upon her with a good courage. Pray you entertain her and conduct your guests in. No?−Mistress bride, will you entreat in the ladies? Your bridegroom is so shamefaced here−

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Will it please your ladyship, madam?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: With the benefit of your company, mistress.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Servant, pray you perform your duties.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: And glad to be commanded, mistress.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: How like you her wit, Mavis?

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Very prettily absolutely well.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: [Trying to take precedence] ’Tis my place.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: You shall pardon me, Mistress Otter.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Why, I am a collegiate.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: But not in ordinary.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: But I am.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: We’ll dispute that within.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Would this had lasted a little longer.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And that they had sent for the heralds. [Enter OTTER.] Captain Otter, what news?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: I have brought my bull, bear and horse in private, and yonder are the trumpeters without, and the drum, gentlemen.

div2.stage: The drum and the trumpets sound.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, Oh, Oh!

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: And we will have a rouse in each of ’em anon, for bold Britons, i’faith.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, Oh, Oh!

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: Follow, follow, follow!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Was there ever poor bridegroom so tormented? Or man, indeed?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: I have not read of the like in the chronicles of the land.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Sure, he cannot but go to a place of rest after all this purgatory.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: He may presume it, I think.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: The spitting, the coughing, the laughter, the neezing, the farting, dancing, noise of the music, and her masculine and loud commanding and urging the whole family, makes him think he has married a Fury.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: And she carries it up bravely.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Ay, she takes any occasion to speak: that’s the height on’t.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: And how soberly Dauphine labours to satisfy him that it was none of his plot!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And has almost brought him to the faith i’the article. [Enter DAUPHINE.] Here he comes.−Where is he now? What’s become of him, Dauphine?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Oh, hold me up a little, I shall go away i’the jest else. He has got on his whole nest of nightcaps, and locked himself up i’the top o’the house, as high as ever he can climb from the noise. I peeped in at a cranny and saw him sitting over a cross-beam o’the roof, like him o’ the saddler’s horse in Fleet Street, upright; and he will sleep there.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: But where are your Collegiates?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Withdrawn with the bride in private.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, they are instructing her i’the college grammar. If she have grace with them, she knows all their secrets instantly.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Methinks the lady Haughty looks well today, for all my dispraise of her in the morning. I think, I shall come about to thee again, Truewit.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Believe it, I told you right. Women ought to repair the losses time and years have made i’ their features with dressings. And an intelligent woman, if she know by herself the least defect, will be most curious to hide it; and it becomes her. If she be short, let her sit much, lest when she stands she be thought to sit. If she have an ill foot, let her wear her gown the longer, and her shoe the thinner. If a fat hand and scald nails, let her carve the less, and act in gloves. If a sour breath, let her never discourse fasting, and always talk at her distance. If she have black and rugged teeth, let her offer the less at laughter, especially if she laugh wide and open.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Oh, you shall have some women, when they laugh, you would think they brayed, it is so rude, and−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Ay, and others, that will stalk i’ their gait like an ostrich, and take huge strides. I cannot endure such a sight. I love measure i’n the feet and number i’n the voice: they are gentlenesses that oftentimes draw no less than the face.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: How cam’st thou to study these creatures so exactly? I would thou wouldst make me a proficient.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, but you must leave to live i’your chamber, then, a month together upon Amadis de Gaula or Don Quixote , as you are wont, and come abroad where the matter is frequent, to court, to tiltings, public shows and feasts, to plays, and church sometimes: thither they come to show their new tires too, to see, and to be seen. In these places a man shall find whom to love, whom to play with, whom to touch once, whom to hold ever. The variety arrests his judgment. A wench to please a man comes not down dropping from the ceiling, as he lies on his back droning a tobacco-pipe. He must go where she is.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Yes, and be never the near.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Out, heretic! That diffidence makes thee worthy it should be so.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: He says true to you, Dauphine.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Why?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: A man should not doubt to overcome any woman. Think he can vanquish’em, and he shall; for though they deny, their desire is to be tempted. Penelope herself cannot hold out long. Ostend, you saw, was taken at last. You must persever and hold to your purpose. They would solicit us, but that they are afraid. Howsoever, they wish in their hearts we should solicit them. Praise’em, flatter ’em, you shall never want eloquence or trust; even the chastest delight to feel themselves that way rubbed. With praises you must mix kisses too. If they take them, they’ll take more. Though they strive, they would be overcome.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Oh, but a man must beware of force.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: It is to them an acceptable violence, and has ofttimes the place of the greatest courtesy. She that might have been forced, and you let her go free without touching, though then she seem to thank you, will ever hate you after; and glad i’ the face, is assuredly sad at the heart.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: But all women are not to be taken all ways.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: ’Tis true. No more than all birds or all fishes. If you appear learned to an ignorant wench, or jocund to a sad, or witty to a foolish, why, she presently begins to mistrust herself. You must approach them i’ their own height, their own line; for the contrary makes many that fear to commit themselves to noble and worthy fellows run into the embraces of a rascal. If she love wit, give verses, though you borrow ’em of a friend, or buy ’em, to have good. If valour, talk of your sword, and be frequent in the mention of quarrels, though you be staunch in fighting. If activity, be seen o’ your barbary often, or leaping over stools, for the credit of your back. If she love good clothes or dressing, have your learned council about you every morning, your French tailor, barber, linener, etcetera. Let your powder, your glass, and your comb be your dearest acquaintance. Take more care for the ornament of your head than the safety; and wish the commonwealth rather troubled than a hair about you. That will take her. Then, if she be covetous and craving, do you promise anything, and perform sparingly; so shall you keep her in appetite still. Seem as you would give, but be like a barren field that fields little, or unlucky dice to foolish and hoping gamesters. Let your gifts be slight and dainty, rather than precious. Let cunning be above cost. Give cherries at time of year, or apricots; and say they were sent you out o’ the country, though you bought ’em in Cheapside. Admire her tires; like her in all fashions, compare her in every habit to some deity, invent excellent dreams to flatter her, and riddles; or, if she be a great one, perform always the second parts to her: like what she likes, praise whom she praises, and fail not to make the household and servants yours, yea, the whole family, and salute ’em by their names (’tis but light cost if you can purchase ’em so) and make her physician your pensioner, and her chief woman. Nor will it be out of your gain to make love to her too, so she follow, not usher, her lady’s pleasure. All blabbing is taken away when she comes to be a part of the crime.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: On what courtly lap hast thou late slept, to come forth so sudden and absolute a courtling?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Good faith, I should rather question you, that are so harkening after these mysteries. I begin to suspect your diligence, Dauphine. Speak, art thou in love in earnest?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Yes, by my troth am I; ’twere ill dissembling before thee.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: With which of ’em, I pray you?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: With all the Collegiates.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Out on thee. We’ll keep you at home, believe it, i’ the stable, an’ you be such a stallion.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: No; I like him well. Men should love wisely, and all women: some one for the face, and let her please the eye; another for the skin, and let her please the touch; and third for the voice, and let her please the ear; and where the objects mix, let the senses so too. Thou wouldst think it strange if I should make ’em all in love with thee afore night!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: I would say thou hadst the best philtre i’ the world, and couldst do more than Madam Medea or Doctor Forman.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: If I do not, let me play the mountebank for my meat while I live, and the bawd for my drink.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: So be it, I say.

div2.head: ACT 4 SCENE 2
div2.stage: [Enter] OTTER, [with his cups], DAW, and LA FOOLE.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Oh lord, gentlemen, how my knights and I have missed you here!

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Why, captain, what service, what service?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: To see me bring up my bull, bear and horse to fight.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Yes, faith, the captain says we shall be his dogs to bait ’em.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: A good employment.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Come on, let’s see a course then.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I am afraid my cousin will be offended if she come.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Be afraid of nothing. Gentlemen, I have placed the drum and the trumpets, and one to give them the sign when you are ready. Here’s my bull for myself, and my bear for Sir John Daw, and my horse for Sir Amorous. Now set your foot to mine, and yours to his, and−

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Pray God my cousin come not.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Saint George and Saint Andrew, fear no cousins. Come, sound, sound. Et rauco strepuerunt cornua cantu .

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Well said, captain, i’faith; well fought at the bull.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Well held at the bear.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: ’Loo, ’loo, captain!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Oh, the horse has kicked off his dog already.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I cannot drink it, as I am a knight.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Gods so! Off with his spurs, somebody.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: It goes against my conscience. My cousin will be angry with it.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I ha’ done mine.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You fought high and fair, Sir John.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: At the head.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Like an excellent bear-dog.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: [To Daw] You take no notice of the business, I hope.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: [To Clerimont] Not a word, sir; you see we are jovial.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Sir Amorous, you must not equivocate. It must be pulled down, for all my cousin.

p.seg: ‘Sfoot, if you take not your drink, they’ll think you are discontented with something; you’ll betray all if you take the least notice.
Not I; I’ll both drink and talk then.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: You must pull the horse on his knees, Sir Amorous. Fear no cousins. Iacta est alea .

p.seg: Oh, now he’s in his vein, and bold. The least hint given him of his wife now will make him rail desperately.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Speak to him of her.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Do you, and I’ll fetch her to the hearing of it.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Captain he-Otter, your she-Otter is coming, your wife.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Wife! buz! Titivilitium . There’s no such thing in nature. I confess, gentlemen, I have a cook, a laundress, a housedrudge, that serves my necessary turns and goes under that title; but he’s an ass that will be so uxorious to tie his affections to one circle. Come, the name dulls appetite. Here, replenish again: another bout. Wives are nasty sluttish animals.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Oh, captain!

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: As ever the earth bare, tribus verbis . Where’s Master Truewit?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: He’s slipped aside, sir.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: But you must drink and be jovial.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Yes, give it me.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: And me too.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Let’s be jovial.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: As jovial as you will.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Agreed. Now you shall ha’ the bear, cousin, and Sir John Daw the horse, and I’ll ha’ the bull still. Sound, Tritons o’ the Thames. Nunc est bibendum, nunc pede libero −

div2.stage: [They drink.]MOROSE speaks from above. The trumpets sounding.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Villains, murderers, sons of the earth and traitors, what do you there?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Oh, now the trumpets have waked him we shall have his company.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: A wife is a scurvy clogdogdo, an unlucky thing, a very foresaid bear-whelp, without any good fashion or breeding: mala bestia .

div2.stage: His wife is brought out to hear him [by TRUEWIT].

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Why did you marry one then, captain?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: A pox!−I married with six thousand pound, I. I was in love with that. I ha’ not kissed my Fury these forty weeks.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: The more to blame you, captain.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, Mistress Otter, hear him a little first.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: She has a breath worse than my grandmother’s, profecto .

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Oh treacherous liar! Kiss me, sweet Master Truewit, and prove him a slandering knave.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I’ll rather believe you, lady.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: And she has a peruke that’s like a pound of hemp made up in shoe-threads.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Oh, viper, mandrake!

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: A most vile face! And yet she spends me forty pound a year in mercury and hogs’ bones. All her teeth were made i’ the Blackfriars, both her eyebrows in the Strand, and her hair in Silver Street. Every part o’ the town owns a piece of her.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: I cannot hold.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: She takes herself asunder still when she goes to bed, into some twenty boxes, and about next day noon is put together again, like a great German clock; and so comes forth and rings a tedious larum to the whole house, and then is quiet again for an hour, but for her quarters.− Ha’ you done me right, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: No, sir, I’ll do you right with my quarters, with my quarters.

div2.stage: She falls upon him ad beats him.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Oh, hold, good princess.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Sound, sound!

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: A battle, a battle!

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: You notorious stinkardly bearward, does my breath smell?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Under correction, dear princess. Look to my bear and my horse, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Do I want teeth and eyebrows, thou bull-dog?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Sound, sound still.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: No, I protest, under correction−

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Ay, now you are under correction, you protest; but you did not protest before correction, sir. Thou Judas, to offer to betray thy princess! I’ll make thee an example−

div2.stage: MOROSE descends with a long sword.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I will have no such examples in my house, Lady Otter.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Ah!

div2.stage: [She runs off, with DAW and LA FOOLE.]

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Mistress Mary Ambree, your examples are dangerous.−Rogues, hell-hounds, Stentors, out of my doors, you sons of noise and tumult, begot on an ill May-day, or when the galley-foist is afloat to Westminster! A trumpeter could not be conceived but then!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: What ails you, sir?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: They have rent my roof, walls and all my windows asunder, with their brazen throats.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Best follow him, Dauphine.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: So I will.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Where’s Daw and La Foole?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: They are both run away, sir. Good gentlemen, help to pacify my princess, and speak to the great ladies for me. Now must I go lie with the bears this fortnight, and keep out o’ the way till my peace be made, for this scandal she has taken. Did you not see my bull-head, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Is’t not on, captain?

p.seg: but he may make a new one, by that is on.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Oh, here ‘tis. An you come over, gentlemen, and ask for Tom Otter, we’ll go down to Ratcliffe, and have a course i’faith, for all these disasters. There’s bona spes left.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Away, captain, get off while you are well.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: I am glad we are rid of him.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You had never been, unless we had put his wife upon him. His humour is as tedious at last, as it was ridiculous at first.

div2.head: ACT 4 SCENE 3
div2.stage: [Enter] HAUGHTY, MISTRESS OTTER, MAVIS, DAW, LA FOOLE, CENTAURE, AND EPICENE. [TRUEWIT and CLERIMONT observe them.]

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: We wondered why you shrieked so, Mistress Otter.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: O God, madam, he came down with a huge long naked weapon in both his hands, and looked so dreadfully! Sure he’s beside himself.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Why, what made you there, Mistress Otter?

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Alas, Mistress Mavis, I was chastising my subject, and thought nothing of him.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: [To Epicene] Faith, mistress, you must do so too. Learn to chastise. Mistress Otter corrects her husband so, he dares not speak but under correction.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: And with his hat off to her: ’twould do you good to see.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: In sadness, ’tis good and mature counsel: practice it, Morose. I’ll call you Morose still now, as I call Centaure and Mavis: we four will be all one.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: And you’ll come to the college and live with us?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Make him give milk and honey.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Look how you manage him at first, you shall have him ever after.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Let him allow you your coach and four horses, your woman, your chambermaid, your page, your gentleman-usher, your French cook, and four grooms.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: And go with us to Bedlam, to the china-houses, and to the Exchange.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: It will open the gate to your fame.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Here’s Centaure has immortalised herself with taming of her wild male.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Ay, she has done the miracle of the kingdom.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: But ladies, do you count it lawful to have such plurality of servants, and do ’em all graces?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Why not? Why should women deny their favours to men? Are they the poorer, or the worse?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Is the Thames the less for the dyer’s water, mistress?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Or a torch for lighting many torches?

p.seg: Well said, La Foole; what a new one he has got!

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: They are empty losses women fear in this kind.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Besides, ladies should be mindful of the approach of age, and let no time want his due use. The best of our days pass first.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: We are rivers, that cannot be called back, madam: she that now excludes her lovers may live to lie a forsaken beldame in a frozen bed.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: ’Tis true, Mavis. And who will wait on us to coach then? or write, or tell us the news then? Make anagrams of our names, and invite us to the cockpit, and kiss our hands all the play-time, and draw their weapons for our honours?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Not one.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Nay, my mistress is not altogether unintelligent of these things; here be in presence have tasted of her favours.

p.seg: What a neighing hobby-horse is this!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: But not with intent to boast ’em again, servant. And have you those excellent receipts, madam, to keep yourselves from bearing of children?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Oh yes, Morose. How should we maintain our youth and beauty else? Many births of a woman make her old, as many crops make the earth barren.

div2.head: ACT 4 SCENE 4

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh my cursed angel, that instructed me to this fate!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Why, sir?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: That I should be seduced by so foolish a devil as a barber will make!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: I would I had been worthy, sir, to have partaken your counsel; you should never have trusted it to such a minister.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Would I could redeem it with the loss of an eye (nephew), a hand, or any other member.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Marry, God forbid, sir, that you should geld yourself to anger your wife.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: So it would rid me of her! And that I did supererogatory penance, in a belfry, at Westminster Hall, i’n the Cockpit, at the fall of a stag, the Tower Wharf (what place is there else?) London Bridge, Paris Garden, Billinsgate, when the noises are at their height and loudest. Nay, I would sit out a play, that were nothing but fights at sea, drum, trumpet and target!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: I hope there shall be no such need, sir. Take patience, good uncle. This is but a day, and ’tis well worn too now.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: O, ’twill be so for ever, nephew, I foresee it, for ever. Strife and tumult are the dowry that comes with a wife.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I told you so, sir, and you would not believe me.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Alas, do not rub those wounds, Master Truewit, to blood again; ’twas my negligence. Add not affliction to affliction. I have perceived the effect of it, too late, in Madam Otter.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: [Coming forward] How do you, sir?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Did you ever hear a more unnecessary question? As if she did not see! Why, I do as you see, empress, empress.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: You are not well, sir! You look very ill! Something has distempered you.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh horrible, monstrous impertinencies! Would not one of these have served? Do you think, sir? Would not one of these have served?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, sir, but these are but notes of female kindness, sir; certain tokens that she has a voice, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, is’t so? Come, and’t be no otherwise−what say you?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: How do you feel yourself, sir?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Again that!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, look you, sir: you would be friends with your wife upon unconscionable terms, her silence−

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: They say you are run mad, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Not for love, I assure you, of you; do you see?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: O lord, gentlemen! Lay hold on him for God’s sake. What shall I do? Who’s his physician (can you tell) that knows the state of his body best, that I might send for him? Good sir, speak. I’ll send for one of my doctors else.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What, to poison me, that I might die intestate and leave you possessed of all?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Lord, how idly he talks, and how his eyes sparkle! He looks green about the temples! Do you see what blue spots he has?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Ay, it’s melancholy.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Gentlemen, for heaven’s sake counsel me. Ladies! Servant, you have read Pliny and Paracelsus: ne’er a word now to comfort a poor gentlewoman? Ay me! What fortune had I to marry a distracted man?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I’ll tell you, mistress−

p.seg: How rarely she holds it up!

div2.stage: [TRUEWIT and CLERIMONT prevent MOROSE from leaving.]

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What mean you, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: What will you tell me, servant?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: The disease in Greek is called mania , in Latin insania , furor , vel ecstasis melancholica , that is, egressio , when a man ex melancholico evadit fanaticus .

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Shall I have a lecture read upon me alive?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: But he may be but phreneticus yet, mistress, and phrenetis is only delirium , or so−

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Ay, that is for the disease, servant; but what is this to the cure? We are sure enough of the disease.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Let me go!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, we’ll entreat her to hold her peace, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh no, labour not to stop her. She is like a conduit-pipe, that will gush out with more force when she opens again.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: I’ll tell you, Morose, you must talk divinity to him altogether, or moral philosophy.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Ay, and there’s an excellent book of moral philosophy, madam, of Reynard the Fox and all the beasts, called Doni’s Philosophy .

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: There is, indeed, sir Amorous La Foole.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh misery!

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I have read it, my lady Centaure, all over to my cousin, here.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Ay, and ’tis a very good book as any is of the moderns.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Tut, he must have Seneca read to him, and Plutarch and the ancients; the moderns are not for this disease.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Why, you discommended them too, today, Sir John.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Ay, in some cases; but in these they are best, and Aristotle’s Ethics .

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Say you so sir John? I think you are deceived: you took it upon trust.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Where’s Trusty, my woman? I’ll end this difference. I prithee, Otter, call her. Her father and mother were both mad when they put her to me.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I think so.−Nay, gentlemen, I am tame. This is but an exercise, I know, a marriage ceremony, which I must endure.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: And one of ’em (I know not which) was cured with the Sick Man’s Salve ; and the other with Greene’s Groat’s-worth of Wit .

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: A very cheap cure, madam.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Ay, it’s very feasible.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: My lady called for you, Mistress Trusty; you must decide a controversy.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Oh, Trusty, which was it you said, your father or your mother, that was cured with the Sick Man’s Salve ?

sp.speaker: TRUSTY
sp.p: My mother, madam, with the Salve .

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Then it was The sick woman’s Salve ?

sp.speaker: TRUSTY
sp.p: And my father with The Groat’s-worth of Wit . But there was other means used: we had a preacher that would preach folk asleep still; and so they were prescribed to go to church by an old woman that was their physician, thrice a week−

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: To sleep?

sp.speaker: TRUSTY
sp.p: Yes, forsooth; and every night they read themselves asleep on those books.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Good faith, it stands with great reason. I would I knew where to procure those books.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh!

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I can help you with one of ’em, Mistress Morose, the Groat’s-worth of Wit .

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: But I shall disfurnish you, Sir Amorous. Can you spare it?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Oh, yes, for a week or so; I’ll read it myself to him.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: No, I must do that, sir; that must be my office.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, oh!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Sure, he would do well enough, if he could sleep.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No, I should do well enough, if you could sleep. Have I no friend that will make her drunk? or give her a little laudanum? or opium?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, sir, she talks ten times worse in her sleep.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Do you not know that, sir? Never ceases all night.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And snores like a porpoise.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, redeem me, fate, redeem me, fate! For how many causes may a man be divorced, nephew?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: I know not, truly, sir.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Some divine must resolve you in that, sir, or canon lawyer.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I will not rest, I will not think of any other hope or comfort, till I know.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Alas, poor man!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You’ll make him mad indeed, ladies, if you pursue this.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: No, we’ll let him breathe now a quarter of an hour or so.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: By my faith, a large truce.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Is that his keeper that is gone with him?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: It is his nephew, madam.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Sir Dauphine Eugenie.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: He looks like a very pitiful knight−

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: As can be. This marriage has put him out of all.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: He has not a penny in his purse, madam−

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: He is ready to cry all this day.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: A very shark, he set me i’n the nick t’other night at primero .

p.seg: How these swabbers talk!
Ay, Otter’s wine has swelled their humours above a spring-tide.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Good Morose, let’s go in again. I like your couches exceeding well; we’ll go lie and talk there.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: I wait on you, madam.

div2.stage: [Exeunt HAUGHTY, CENTAURE, MAVIS, TRUSTY, DAW and LA FOOLE.]

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: ’Slight, I will have ’em as silent as signs, and their posts too, ere I ha’ done. Do you hear, lady bride? I pray thee now, as thou art a noble wench, continue this discourse of Dauphine within; but praise him exceedingly. Magnify him with all the height of affection thou canst (I have some purpose in’t) and but beat off these two rooks, Jack Daw and his fellow, with any discontentment hither, and I’ll honour thee for ever.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: I was about it here. It angered me to the soul to hear ’em begin to talk so malapert.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Pray thee perform it, and thou win’st me an idolater to thee everlasting.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Will you go in and hear me do it?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: No, I’ll stay here. Drive ’em out of your company, ’tis all I ask; which cannot be any way better done than by extolling Dauphine, whom they have so slighted.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: I warrant you; you shall expect one of ’em presently.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: What a cast of kestrils are these, to hawk after ladies thus!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Ay, and strike at such an eagle as Dauphine.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: He will be mad when we tell him. Here he comes.

div2.head: ACT 4 SCENE 5

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: O sir, you are welcome.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Where’s thine uncle?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Run out o’ doors in’s nightcaps to talk with a casuist about his divorce. It works admirably.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Thou wouldst ha’ said so if thou hadst been here! The ladies have laughed at thee most comically since thou went’st, Dauphine.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: And asked if thou wert thine uncle’s keeper.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And the brace of baboons answered yes, and said thou wert a pitiful poor fellow and didst live upon posts, and hadst nothing but three suits of apparel and some few benevolences that lords ga’ thee to fool to ’em and swagger.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Let me not live, I’ll beat them. I’ll bind ’em both to grand madam’s bed-posts and have ’em baited with monkeys.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Thou shalt not need, they shall be beaten to thy hand, Dauphine. I have an execution to serve upon ’em I warrant thee shall serve: trust my plot.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Ay, you have many plots! So you had one to make all the wenches in love with me.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, if I do not yet afore night, as near as ’tis, and that they do not every one invite thee and be ready to scratch for thee, take the mortgage of my wit.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: ’Fore God, I’ll be his witness; thou shalt have it, Dauphine; thou shalt be his fool for ever if thou dost not.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Agreed. Perhaps ’twill be the better estate. Do you observe this gallery, or rather lobby, indeed? Here are a couple of studies, at each end one: here will I act such a tragicomedy between the Guelphs and the Ghibellines, Daw and La Foole. Which of ’em comes out first will I seize on. (You two shall be the chorus behind the arras, and whip out between the acts and speak.) If I do not make ’em keep the peace for this remnant of the day, if not of the year, I have failed once−I hear Daw coming. Hide, and do not laugh, for God’s sake.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Which is the way into the garden, trow?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, Jack Daw! I am glad I have met with you. In good faith, I must have this matter go no further between you. I must ha’ it taken up.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: What matter, sir? Between whom?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Come, you disguise it: Sir Amorous and you. If you love me, Jack, you shall make use of your philosophy now, for this once, and deliver me your sword. This is not the wedding the Centaurs were at, though there be a she-one here. The bride has entreated me I will see no blood shed at her bridal; you saw her whisper me erewhile.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: As I hope to finish Tacitus, I intend no murder.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Do you not wait for Sir Amorous?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Not I, by my knighthood.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And your scholarship too?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: And my scholarship too.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Go to, then I return you your sword, and ask you mercy; but put it not up, for you will be assaulted. [Returns his sword.] I understood that you had apprehended it, and walked here to brave him, and that you had held your life contemptible in regard of your honour.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: No, no, no such thing, I assure you. He and I parted now as good friends as could be.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Trust not you to that visor. I saw him since dinner with another face. I have known many men in my time vexed with losses, with deaths, and with abuses, but so offended a wight as Sir Amorous did I never see, or read of. For taking away his guests, sir, today, that’s the cause, and he declares it behind your back with such threat’nings and contempts. He said to Dauphine you were the arrant’st ass−

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Ay, he may say his pleasure.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And swears you are so protested a coward that he knows you will never do him any manly or single right, and therefore he will take his course.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I’ll give him any satisfaction, sir−but fighting.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Ay, sir, but who knows what satisfaction he’ll take? Blood he thirsts for, and blood he will have; and whereabouts on you he will have it, who knows but himself?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I pray you, Master Truewit, be you a mediator.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Well, sir, conceal yourself then in this study till I return. [He puts him up.] Nay, you must be content to be locked in; for, for mine own reputation, I would not have you seen to receive a public disgrace, while I have the matter in managing. Gods so, here he comes! Keep your breath close, that he do not hear you sigh.−In good faith, Sir Amorous, he is not this way; I pray you be merciful, do not murder him; he is a Christian as good as you; you are armed as if you sought a revenge on all his race. Good Dauphine, get him away from this place. I never knew a man’s choler so high but he would speak to his friends, he would hear reason.−Jack Daw, Jack Daw! Asleep!

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: [Within] Is he gone, Master Truewit?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Ay, did you hear him?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Oh God! yes.

p.seg: What a quick ear fear has!

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: [Comes out of the study.] But is he so armed, as you say?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Armed? Did you ever see a fellow set out to take possession?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Ay, sir.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: That may give you some light to conceive of him; but ’tis nothing to the principal. Some false brother i’ the house has furnished him strangely. Or, if it were out o’ the house, it was Tom Otter.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Indeed he’s a captain, and his wife is his kinswoman.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: He has got somebody’s old two-hand sword, to mow you off at the knees. And that sword hath spawned such a dagger!− But then he is so hung with pikes, halberds, petronels, calivers and muskets, that he looks like a justice of peace’s hall; a man of two thousand a year, is not cessed at so many weapons as he has on. There was never fencer challenged at so many several foils. You would think he meant to murder all Saint Pulchre’s parish. If he could but victual himself for half a year in his breeches, he is sufficiently armed to overrun a country.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Good lord! what means he, sir? I pray you, Master Truewit, be you a mediator.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Well, I’ll try if he will be appeased with a leg or an arm; if not, you must die once.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I would be loath to lose my right arm, for writing madrigals.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, if he will be satisfied with a thumb or a little finger, all’s one to me. You must think I’ll do my best.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Good sir, do.

div2.stage: He puts him up again, and then [DAUPHINE and CLERIMONT] come forth.]

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: What hast thou done?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: He will let me do nothing, man, he does all afore me; he offers his left arm.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: His left wing for a Jack Daw.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Take it by all means.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: How! Maim a man for ever for a jest? What a conscience hast thou?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: ’Tis no loss to him: he has no employment for his arms but to eat spoon-meat. Beside, as good maim his body as his reputation.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: He is a scholar and a Wit, and yet he does not think so. But he loses no reputation with us, for we all resolved him an ass before. To your places again.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: I pray thee let me be in at the other a little.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Look, you’ll spoil all: these be ever your tricks.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: No, but I could hit of some things that thou wilt miss, and thou wilt say are good ones.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I warrant you. I pray forbear, I will leave it off else.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Come away, Clerimont.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Sir Amorous!

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Master Truewit.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Whither were you going?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Down into the court to make water.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: By no means, sir; you shall rather tempt your breeches.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Why, sir?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: [Opening the door of the other study.] Enter here if you love your life.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Why? Why?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Question till your throat be cut, do; dally till the enraged soul find you.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Who’s that?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Daw it is; will you in?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Ay, ay, I’ll in; what’s the matter?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, if he had been cool enough to tell us that, there had been some hope to atone you, but he seems so implacably enraged!

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: ’Slight, let him rage! I’ll hide myself.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Do, good sir. But what have you done to him within that should provoke him thus? You have broke some jest upon him afore the ladies−

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Not I, never in my life broke jest upon any man. The bride was praising Sir Dauphine, and he went away in snuff, and I followed him, unless he took offence at me in his drink erewhile, that I would not pledge all the horse-full.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: By my faith, and that may be, you remember well; but he walks the round up and down, through every room o’ the house, with a towel in his hand, crying, ‘Where’s La Foole? Who saw La−Foole?’ And when Dauphine and I demanded the cause, we can force no answer from him but ‘O revenge, how sweet art thou! I will strangle him in this towel’−which leads us to conjecture that the main cause of his fury is for bringing your meat today, with a towel about you, to his discredit.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Like enough. Why, and he be angry for that, I’ll stay here till his anger be blown over.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: A good becoming resolution, sir. If you can put it on o’ the sudden.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Yes, I can put it on. Or I’ll away into the country presently.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: How will you get out o’the house, sir? He knows you are i’the house, and he’ll watch you this se’en-night but he’ll have you. He’ll outwait a sergeant for you.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Why then I’ll stay here.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You must think how to victual yourself in time then.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Why, sweet Master Truewit, will you entreat my cousin Otter to send me a cold venison pasty, a bottle or two of wine, and a chamber-pot?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: A stool were better, sir, of Sir A-jax his invention.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Ay, that will be better indeed; and a pallet to lie on.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, I would not advise you to sleep by any means.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Would you not, sir? Why then I will not.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yet there’s another fear−

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Is there, sir? What is’t?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: No, he cannot break open this door with his foot, sure.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I’ll set my back against it, sir. I have a good back.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: But then if he should batter.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Batter! If he dare, I’ll have an action of batt’ry against him.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Cast you the worst. He has sent for powder already, and what he will do with it, no man knows; perhaps blow up the corner o’ the house where he suspects you are. Here he comes! In, quickly. [He feigns as if one were present, to fight the other, who is run in to hide himself.] I protest, Sir John Daw, he is not this way. What will you do? Before God, you shall hang no petard here. I’ll die rather. Will you not take my word? I never knew one but would be satisfied.−Sir Amorous, there’s no standing out. He has made a petard of an old brass pot, to force your door. Think upon some satisfaction or terms to offer him.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: [Within.] Sir, I’ll give him any satisfaction. I dare give any terms.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You’ll leave it to me then?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Ay, sir. I’ll stand to any conditions.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: How now, what think you, sirs? Were’t not a difficult thing to determine which of these two feared most?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Yes, but this fears the bravest; the other a whiniling dastard, Jack Daw. But La Foole, a brave heroic coward! And is afraid in a great look and a stout accent. I like him rarely.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Had it not been pity these two should ha’ been concealed?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Shall I make a motion?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Briefly. For I must strike while ’tis hot.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Shall I go fetch the ladies to the catastrophe?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Umh? Ay, by my troth.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: By no mortal means. Let them continue in the state of ignorance, and err still; think ’em wits and fine fellows as they have done. ’Twere sin to reform them.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Well, I will have ‘em fetched, now I think on’t, for a private purpose of mine; do, Clerimont, fetch ’em, and discourse to ’em all that’s past, and bring ’em into the gallery here.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: This is thy extreme vanity now; thou think’st thou wert undone if every jest thou mak’st were not published.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Thou shalt see how unjust thou art presently. Clerimont, say it was Dauphine’s plot. [Exit CLERIMONT.] Trust me not if the whole drift be not for thy good. There’s a carpet i’ the next room; put it on, with this scarf over thy face and a cushion o’ thy head, and be ready when I call Amorous. Away− [Exit DAUPHINE.] John Daw!

div2.stage: [He brings DAW out of his study.]

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: What good news, sir?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Faith, I have followed and argued with him hard for you. I told him you were a knight and a scholar, and that you knew fortitude did consist magis patiendo quam faciendo, magis ferendo quam feriendo .

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: It doth so indeed, sir.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And that you would suffer, I told him: so at first he demanded, by my troth, in my conceit too much.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: What was it, sir?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Your upper lip, and six o’ your fore-teeth.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: ’Twas unreasonable.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, I told him plainly, you could not spare ’em all. So after long argument ( pro et con , as you know) I brought him down to your two butter-teeth, and them he would have.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Oh, did you so? Why, he shall have ’em.

div2.stage: [Enter above HAUGHTY, CENTAURE, MAVIS, MISTRESS OTTER, EPICENE, TRUSTY and CLERIMONT]

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: But he shall not, sir, by your leave. The conclusion is this, sir: because you shall be very good friends hereafter, and this never to be remembered or upbraided, besides that he may not boast he has done any such thing to you in his own person, he is to come here in disguise, give you five kicks in private, sir, take your sword from you, and lock you up in that study, during pleasure. Which will be but a little while, we’ll get it released presently.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Five kicks? He shall have six, sir, to be friends.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Believe me, you shall not overshoot yourself to send him that word by me.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Deliver it, sir. He shall have it with all my heart, to be friends.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Friends? Nay, and he should not be so, and heartily too, upon these terms, he shall have me to enemy while I live. Come, sir, bear it bravely.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: O God, sir, ’tis nothing.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: True. Whats’s six kicks to a man that reads Seneca?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I have had a hundred, sir.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Sir Amorous! No speaking one to another, or rehearsing old matters.

div2.stage: DAUPHINE [masked with a scarf] comes forth and kicks him.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: One, two, three, four, five. I protest, Sir Amorous, you shall have six.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, I told you, you should not talk. Come, give him six, an he will needs. [DAUPHINE kicks him again.] Your swords. [DAW gives TRUEWIT his sword.] Now return to your safe custody: you shall presently meet afore the ladies, and be the dearest friends one to another− [DAW goes into his study.] Give me the scarf; now thou shalt beat the other barefaced. Stand by, Sir Amorous!

div2.stage: [Exit DAUPHINE; TRUEWIT brings out LA FOOLE.]

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: What’s here? A sword!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I cannot help it, without I should take the quarrel upon myself; here he has sent you his sword−

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I’ll receive none on’t.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: And he wills you to fasten it against a wall, and break your head in some few several places against the hilts.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I will not: tell him roundly. I cannot endure to shed my own blood.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Will you not?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: No. I’ll beat it against a fair flat wall, if that will satisfy him; if not, he shall beat it himself for Amorous.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, this is strange starting off, when a man undertakes for you! I offered him another condition: will you stand to that?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Ay, what is’t?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: That you will be beaten in private.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Yes. I am content, at the blunt.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Then you must submit yourself to be hoodwinked in this scarf, and be led to him, where he will take your sword from you, and make you bear a blow over the mouth, gules , and tweaks by the nose sans nombre .

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I am content. But why must I be blinded?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: That’s for your good, sir: because, if he should grow insolent upon this and publish it hereafter to your disgrace (which I hope he will not do) you might swear safely and protest he never beat you, to your knowledge.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Oh, I conceive.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: I do not doubt but you’ll be perfect good friends upon’t, and not dare to utter an ill thought one of another in future.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Not I, as God help me, of him.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nor he of you, sir. If he should−Come, sir. [Blindfolds him.] All hid, Sir John.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Oh, Sir John, Sir John! Oh, Oh, Oh, Oh, Oh, Oh, Oh−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Good, Sir John, leave tweaking, you’ll blow his nose off. [Exit DAUPHINE with the two swords.] ’Tis Sir John’s pleasure you should retire into the study. [Unbinds LA FOOLE’s eyes and shuts him in.] Why, now you are friends. All bitterness between you, I hope, is buried; you shall come forth by and by Damon and Pythias upon’t, and embrace with all the rankness of friendship that can be. [Enter DAUPHINE.] I trust we shall have ’em tamer i’their language hereafter. Dauphine, I worship thee.−God’s will, the ladies have surprised us!

div2.head: ACT 4 SCENCE 6
div2.stage: [Enter] HAUGHTY, CENTAURE, MAVIS, MISTRESS OTTER, EPICENE, TRUSTY [and CLERIMONT], having discovered part of the past scene, above.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Centaure, how our judgments were imposed on by these adulterate knights!

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Nay, madam, Mavis was more deceived than we; ’twas her commendation uttered ’em in the college.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: I commended but their wits, madam, and their braveries. I never looked toward their valours.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Sir Dauphine is valiant, and a Wit too, it seems.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: And a Bravery too.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Was this his project?

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: So Master Clerimont intimates, madam.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Good Morose, when you come to the college, will you bring him with you? He seems a very perfect gentleman.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: He is so, madam, believe it.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: But when will you come, Morose?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Three or four days hence, madam, when I have got me a coach and horses.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: No, tomorrow, good Morose; Centaure shall send you her coach.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Yes, faith, do, and bring Sir Dauphine with you.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: She has promised that, Mavis.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: He is a very worthy gentleman in his exteriors, madam.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Ay, he shows he is judicial in his clothes.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: And yet not so superlatively neat as some, madam, that have their faces set in a brake!

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Ay, and have every hair in form!

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: That wear purer linen then ourselves, and profess more neatness than the French hermaphrodite!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Ay, ladies, they; what they tell one of us, have told a thousand, and are the only thieves of our fame; that think to take us with that perfume or with that lace, and laugh at us unconscionably when they have done.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: But Sir Dauphine’s carelessness becomes him.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: I could love a man for such a nose!

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Or such a leg!

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: He has an exceeding good eye, madam!

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: And a very good lock!

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Good Morose, bring him to my chamber first.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Please your honours to meet at my house, madam?

p.seg: See how they eye thee, man! They are taken, I warrant thee.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: [Approaching Truewit and Dauphine.] You have unbraced our brace of knights here, Master Truewit.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Not I, madam, it was sir Dauphine’s engine; who, if he have disfurnished your ladyship of any guard or service by it, is able to make the place good again in himself.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: There’s no suspicion of that, sir.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: God so, Mavis, Haughty is kissing.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Let us go too and take part.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: But I am glad of the fortune (beside the discovery of two such empty caskets) to gain the knowledge of so rich a mine of virtue as Sir Dauphine.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: We would be all glad to style him of our friendship, and see him at the college.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: He cannot mix with a sweeter society, I’ll prophesy, and I hope he himself will think so.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: I should be rude to imagine otherwise, lady.

p.seg: Did not I tell thee, Dauphine? Why, all their actions are governed by crude opinion, without reason or cause; they know not why they do anything; but as they are informed, believe, judge, praise, condemn, love, hate, and in emulation one of another, do all these things alike. Only, they have a natural inclination sways ’em generally to the worst, when they are left to themselves. But pursue it, now thou hast ’em.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Shall we go in again, Morose?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Yes, madam.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: We’ll entreat Sir Dauphine’s company.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Stay, good madam, the interview of the two friends, Pylades and Orestes: I’ll fetch ‘em out to you straight.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Will you, Master Truewit?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Ay, but noble ladies, do not confess in your countenance or outward bearing to ’em any discovery of their follies, that we may see how they will bear up again, with what assurance and erection.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: We will not, Sir Dauphine.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE [and] MAVIS
sp.p: Upon our honours, Sir Dauphine.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Sir Amorous, Sir Amorous! The ladies are here.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: [Within] Are they?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, but slip out by and by as their backs are turned and meet Sir John here, as by chance, when I call you.− Jack Daw!

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: [Within] What say you, sir?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Whip out behind me suddenly, and no anger i’ your looks to your adversary.−Now, now!

div2.stage: [LA FOOLE and DAW come out of their studies, and salute each other.]

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Noble Sir John Daw! Where ha’ you been?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: To seek you, Sir Amorous.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Me! I honour you.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I prevent you, sir.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: They have forgot their rapiers!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, they meet in peace, man.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Where’s your sword, Sir John?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: And yours, sir Amorous?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Mine? My boy had it forth to mend the handle, e’en now.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: And my gold handle was broke too, and my boy had it forth.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Indeed, sir? How their excuses meet!

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: What a consent there is i’ the handles!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, there is so i’ the points too, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Oh me! Madam, he comes again, the madman! Away!

div2.stage: [Exeunt hastily HAUGHTY, CENTAURE, EPICENE, MAVIS, MISTRESS OTTER, TRUSTY, DAW and LA FOOLE.]

div2.head: ACT 4 SCENE 7
div2.stage: [Enter] MOROSE [with a sword in each hand;] he had found the two swords drawn within.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What make these naked weapons here, gentlemen?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, sir! Here hath like to been murder since you went! A couple of knights fallen out about the bride’s favours. We were fain to take away their weapons, your house had been begged by this time else−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: For what?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: For manslaughter, sir, as being accessary.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: And for her favours?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Ay, sir, heretofore, not present. Clerimont, carry ’em their swords now. They have done all the hurt they will do.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Ha’you spoke with the lawyer, sir?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh no! There is such a noise i’ the court that they have frighted me home with more violence then I went! Such speaking and counter-speaking, with their several voices of citations, appellations, allegations, certificates, attachments, intergatories, references, convictions, and afflictions indeed, among the doctors and proctors, that the noise here is silence to’t! A kind of calm midnight!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, sir, if you would be resolved indeed, I can bring you hither a very sufficient lawyer and a learned divine, that shall enquire into every least scruple for you.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Can you, Master Truewit?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, and are very sober grave persons, that will dispatch it in a chamber, with a whisper or two.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Good sir, shall I hope this benefit from you, and trust myself into your hands?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Alas, sir! Your nephew and I have been ashamed, and oft-times mad, since you went, to think how you are abused. Go in, good sir, and lock yourself up till we call you; we’ll tell you more anon, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Do your pleasure with me gentlemen; I believe in you, and that deserves no delusion−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You shall find none, sir− [Exit Morose] but heaped, heaped plenty of vexation.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: What wilt thou do now, Wit?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Recover me hither Otter and the barber if you can, by any means, presently.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Why? To what purpose?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, I’ll make the deepest divine and gravest lawyer out o’ them two for him−

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Thou canst not, man; these are waking dreams.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Do not fear me. Clap but a civil gown with a welt o’ the one, and a canonical cloak with sleeves o’ the other, and give ’em a few terms i’ their mouths; if there come not forth as able a doctor and complete a parson for this turn as may be wished, trust not my election. And I hope, without wronging the dignity of either profession, since they are but persons put on, and for mirth’s sake, to torment him. The barber smatters Latin, I remember.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Yes, and Otter too.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Well then, if I make ’em not wrangle out this case to his no comfort, let me be thought a Jack Daw, or La Foole, or anything worse. Go you to your ladies, but first send for them.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: I will.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Where had you our swords, Master Clerimont?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Why, Dauphine took ’em from the madman.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: And he took ’em from our boys, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Very like, sir.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Thank you, good Master Clerimont. Sir John Daw and I are both beholden to you.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Would I knew how to make you so, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Sir Amorous and I are your servants, sir.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Gentlemen, have any of you a pen and ink? I would fain write out a riddle in Italian for Sir Dauphine to translate.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Not I, in troth, lady, I am no scrivener.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I can furnish you, I think, lady.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: He has it in the haft of a knife, I believe!

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: No, he has his box of instruments.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Like a surgeon!

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: For the mathematics: his square, his compasses, his brass pens, and black lead, to draw maps of every place and person where he comes.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: How, maps of persons!

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Yes, sir, of Nomentack, when he was here, and of the Prince of Moldavia, and of his mistress, Mistress Epicene.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Away! He has not found out her latitude, I hope.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: You are a pleasant gentleman, sir.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Faith, now we are in private, let’s wanton it a little and talk waggishly. Sir John, I am telling Sir Amorous here that you two govern the ladies; where’er you come, you carry the feminine gender afore you.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: They shall rather carry us afore them, if they will, sir.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Nay, I believe that they do, withal; but that you are the prime men in their affections, and direct all their actions−

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Not I; Sir Amorous is.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I protest, Sir John is.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: As I hope to rise in the state, Sir Amorous, you ha’ the person.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Sir John, you ha’ the person, and the discourse too.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Not I, sir. I have no discourse−and then you have activity beside.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I protest, Sir John, you come as high from Tripoly as I do every whit, and lift as many joined stools and leap over ’em, if you would use it−

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Well, agree on’t together, knights, for between you you divide the kingdom or commonwealth of ladies’ affections: I see it and can perceive a little how they observe you, and fear you, indeed. You could tell strange stories, my masters, if you would, I know.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Faith, we have seen somewhat, sir.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: That we have: velvet petticoats and wrought smocks or so.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Ay, and−

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Nay, out with it, Sir John; do not envy your friend the pleasure of hearing, when you have had the delight of tasting.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Why−a−you speak, Sir Amorous.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: No, do you, Sir John Daw.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: I’ faith, you shall.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I’ faith, you shall.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Why, we have been−

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: In the great bed at Ware together in our time. On, Sir John.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Nay, do you, Sir Amorous.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: And these ladies with you, knights?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: No, excuse us, sir.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: We must not wound reputation.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: No matter; they were these, or others. Our bath cost us fifteen pound, when we came home.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
