sp.p: Do you hear, Sir John, you shall tell me but one thing truly, as you love me.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: If I can, I will, sir.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: You lay in the same house with the bride here?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Yes, and conversed with her hourly, sir.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: And what humour is she of? Is she coming and open, free?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Oh, exceeding open, sir. I was her servant, and Sir Amorous was to be.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Come, you have both had favours from her? I know and have heard so much.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Oh no, sir.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: You shall excuse us, sir: we must not wound reputation.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Tut, she is married now, and you cannot hurt her with any report, and therefore speak plainly: how many times, i’ faith? Which of you led first? Ha?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Sir John had her maidenhead, indeed.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Oh, it pleases him to say so, sir, but Sir Amorous knows what is what as well.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Dost thou i’faith, Amorous?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: In a manner, sir.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Why, I commend you lads. Little knows Don Bridegroom of this. Nor shall he, for me.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Hang him, mad ox.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Speak softly: here comes his nephew, with the Lady Haughty. He’ll get the ladies from you, sirs, if you look not to him in time.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Why, if he do, we’ll fetch them home again, I warrant you.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: I assure you, Sir Dauphine, it is the price and estimation of your virtue only that hath embarked me to this adventure, and I could not but make out to tell you so; nor can I repent me of the act, since it is always an argument of some virtue in ourselves that we love and affect it so in others.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Your ladyship sets too high a price on my weakness.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Sir, I can distinguish gems from pebbles−

p.seg: Are you so skilful in stones?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: And howsover I may suffer in such a judgment as yours, by admitting equality of rank or society with Centaure or Mavis−

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: You do not, madam; I perceive they are your mere foils.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Then are you a friend to truth, sir. It makes me love you the more. It is not the outward but the inward man that I affect. They are not apprehensive of an eminent perfection, but love flat and dully.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: [Within.] Where are you, my lady Haughty?

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: I come presently, Centaure.−My chamber, sir, my page shall show you; and Trusty, my woman, shall be ever awake for you; you need not fear to communicate anything with her, for she is a Fidelia. I pray you wear this jewel for my sake, sir Dauphine. [Enter CENTAURE.] Where’s Mavis, Centaure?

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Within, madam, a-writing. I’ll follow you presently. I’ll but speak a word with Sir Dauphine.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: With me, madam?

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Good Sir Dauphine, do not trust Haughty, nor make any credit to her, whatever you do besides. Sir Dauphine, I give you this caution: she is a perfect courtier and loves nobody but for her uses; and for her uses she loves all. Besides, her physicians give her out to be none o’ the clearest−whether she pay ’em or no, heav’n knows; and she’s above fifty too, and pargets! See her in a forenoon. Here comes Mavis, a worse face then she! You would not like this by candlelight. If you’ll come to my chamber one o’ these mornings early, or late in an evening, I’ll tell you more. [Enter MAVIS.] Where’s Haughty, Mavis?

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Within, Centaure.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: What ha’ you there?

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: An Italian riddle for Sir Dauphine. (You shall not see it i’faith, Centaure.) Good sir Dauphine, solve it for me. I’ll call for it anon.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: How now, Dauphine? How dost thou quit thyself of these females?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: ’Slight, they haunt me like fairies, and give me jewels here; I cannot be rid of ’em.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Oh, you must not tell though.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Mass, I forgot that; I was never so assaulted. One loves for virtue, and bribes me with this. Another loves me with caution, and so would possess me. A third brings me a riddle here, and all are jealous and rail each at other.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: A riddle? Pray’ le’ me see’t? He reads the paper. Sir Dauphine, I chose this way of intimation for privacy. The ladies here, I know, have both hope and purpose to make a collegiate and servant of you. If I might be so honoured as to appear at any end of so noble a work, I would enter into a fame of taking physic tomorrow and continue it four or five days or longer, for your visitation. Mavis. −By my faith, a subtle one! Call you this a riddle? What’s their plain dealing, trow?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: We lack Truewit to tell us that.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: We lack him for somewhat else too: his knights reformados are wound up as high and insolent as ever they were.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: You jest.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: No drunkards, either with wine or vanity, ever confessed such stories of themselves. I would not give a fly’s leg in balance against all the women’s reputations here, if they could be but thought to speak truth; and for the bride, they have made their affidavit against her directly−

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: What, that they have lain with her?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Yes; and tell times and circumstances, with the cause why and the place where. I had almost brought ’em to affirm that they had done it today.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Not both of ’em?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Yes, faith; with a sooth or two more I had effected it. They would ha’ set it down under their hands.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Why, they will be our sport, I see, still! Whether we will or no.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, are you here? Come, Dauphine. Go call your uncle presently. I have fitted my divine and my canonist, dyed their beards and all; the knaves do not know themselves, they are so exalted and altered. Preferment changes any man. Thou shalt keep one door and I another, and then Clerimont in the midst, that he may have no means of escape from their cavilling when they grow hot once. And then the women (as I have given the bride her instructions) to break in upon him i’ the l’envoy . Oh, ‘twill be full and twanging! Away, fetch him. [Exit DAUPHINE.]Enter CUTBEARD disguised as a canon lawyer, OTTER as a divine.] Come, master doctor and master parson, look to your parts now and discharge ’em bravely; you are well set forth, perform it as well. If you chance to be out, do not confess it with standing still or humming or gaping one at another, but go on and talk aloud and eagerly, use vehement action, and only remember your terms, and you are safe. Let the matter go where it will: you have many will do so. But at first be very solemn and grave like your garments, though you loose yourselves after and skip out like a brace of jugglers on a table. Here he comes! Set your faces, and look superciliously while I present you.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Are these the two learned men?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, sir; please you salute ’em?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Salute ’em? I had rather do anything than wear out time so unfruitfully, sir. I wonder how these common forms, as ‘God save you’ and ‘You are welcome’, are come to be a habit in our lives! Or ‘I am glad to see you!’ when I cannot see what the profit can be of these words, so long as it is no whit better with him whose affairs are sad and grievous that he hears this salutation.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: ’Tis true, sir; we’ll go to the matter then. Gentlemen, master doctor and master parson, I have acquainted you sufficiently with the business for which you are come hither. And you are not now to inform yourselves in the state of the question, I know. This is the gentleman who expects your resolution, and therefore, when you please, begin.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Please you, master doctor.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Please you, good master parson.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: I would hear the canon law speak first.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: It must give place to positive divinity, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Nay, good gentlemen, do not throw me into circumstances. Let your comforts arrive quickly at me, those that are. Be swift in affording me my peace, if so I shall hope any. I love not your disputations or your court tumults. And that it be not strange to you, I will tell you. My father, in my education, was wont to advise me that I should always collect and contain my mind, not suff’ring it to flow loosely; that I should look to what things were necessary to the carriage of my life, and what not, embracing the one and eschewing the other. In short, that I should endear myself to rest and avoid turmoil: which now is grown to be another nature to me. So that I come not to your public pleadings, or your places of noise; not that I neglect those things that make for the dignity of the commonwealth, but for the mere avoiding of clamours and impertinencies of orators, that know not how to be silent. And for the cause of noise am I now a suitor to you. You do not know in what a misery I have been exercised this day, what a torrent of evil! My very house turns round with the tumult! I dwell in a windmill! The perpetual motion is here, and not at Eltham.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Well, good master doctor, will you break the ice? Master parson will wade after.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Sir, though unworthy, and the weaker, I will presume.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: ’Tis no presumption, domine doctor.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Yet again!

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Your question is, for how many causes a man may have divortium legitimum , a lawful divorce. First, you must understand the nature of the word, divorce, a divertendo −

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No excursions upon words, good doctor; to the question briefly.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: I answer then, the canon law affords divorce but in few cases, and the principal is in the common case, the adulterous case: But there are duodecim impedimenta , twelve impediments (as we call ’em) all which do not dirimere contractum , but irritum reddere matrimonium , as we say in the canon law, not take away the bond, but cause a nullity therein.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I understood you before; good sir, avoid your impertinency of translation.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: He cannot open this too much, sir, by your favour.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Yet more!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Oh, you must give the learned men leave, sir. To your impediments, master doctor.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The first is impedimentum erroris .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Of which there are several species.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Ay, as error personae .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: If you contract yourself to one person, thinking her another.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Then, error fortunae .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: If she be a beggar, and you thought her rich.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Then, error qualitatis .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: If she prove stubborn or headstrong, that you thought obedient.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: How? Is that, sir, a lawful impediment? One at once, I pray you, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay, ante copulam , but not post copulam , sir.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Master parson says right. Nec post nuptiarum benedictionem . It doth indeed but irrita reddere sponsalia , annul the contract; after marriage it is of no obstancy.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Alas, sir, what a hope are we fall’n from, by this time!

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The next is conditio : if you thought her freeborn, and she prove a bondwoman, there is impediment of estate and condition.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay, but master doctor, those servitudes are sublatae now, among us Christians.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: By your favour, master parson−

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: You shall give me leave, master doctor.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Nay, gentlemen, quarrel not in that question; it concerns not my case:pass to the third.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Well then, the third is votum . If either party have made a vow of chastity. But that practice, as master parson said of the other, is taken away among us, thanks be to discipline. The fourth is cognatio : if the persons be of kin within the degrees.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay. Do you know what the degrees are, sir?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No, nor I care not, sir; they offer me no comfort in the question, I am sure.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: But there is a branch of this impediment may, which is cognatio spiritualis . If you were her godfather, sir, then the marriage is incestuous.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: That comment is absurd and superstitious, master doctor. I cannot endure it. Are we not all brothers and sisters, and as much akin in that as godfathers and god-daughters?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh me! To end the controversy, I never was a godfather, I never was a godfather in my life, sir. Pass to the next.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The fifth is crimen adulterii : the known case. The sixth, cultus disparitas , difference of religion: have you ever examined her what religion she is of?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No, I would rather she were of none, than be put to the trouble of it!

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: You may have it done for you, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: By no means, good sir; on to the rest. Shall you ever come to an end, think you?

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Yes, he has done half, sir. (On to the rest.) Be patient and expect, sir.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The seventh is vis : if it were upon compulsion or force.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh no, it was too voluntary, mine; too voluntary.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The eight is ordo : if ever she have taken holy orders.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: That’s supersitious too.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: No matter, master parson: would she would go into a nunnery yet.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The ninth is ligament : if you were bound, sir, to any other before.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I thrust myself too soon into these fetters.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The tenth is publica honestas , which is inchoate quaedam affinitas .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay, or affinitas orta ex sponsalibus , and is but leve impedimentum .

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I feel no air of comfort blowing to me in all this.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The eleventh is affinitas ex fornicatione .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Which is no less vera affinitas , than the other, master doctor.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: True, quae oritur ex legitimo matrimonio .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: You say right, venerable doctor. And nascitur ex eo, quod per conjugium duae personae efficiuntur una caro −

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Heyday, now they begin.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: I conceive you, master parson. Ita per fornicationem aeque est verus pater, qui sic generat −

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Et vere filius qui sic generatur −

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What’s all this to me?

p.seg: Now it grows warm.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: The twelfth and last is si forte coire nequibis .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay, that is impedimentum gravissimum . It doth utterly annul and annihilate, that. If you have manifestam frigiditatem , you are well, sir.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, there is comfort come at length, sir. Confess yourself but a man unable, and she will sue to be divorced first.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay, or if there be morbus perpetuus et insanabilis ; as paralysis, elephantiasis, or so−

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Oh, but frigiditas is the fairer way, gentlemen.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: You say troth, sir, and as it is in the canon, master doctor.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: I conceive you, sir.

p.seg: Before he speaks!

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: That ‘a boy or child under years is not fit for marriage because he cannot reddere debitum’ . So your omnipotentes −

p.seg: Your impotentes , you whoreson lobster.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Your impotentes , I should say, are minime apti ad contrahenda matrimonium .

p.seg: Matrimonium ? We shall have most unmatrimonial Latin with you: matrimonia , and be hanged.
You put ’em out, man.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: But then there will arise a doubt, master parson, in our case, post matrimonium : that frigiditate praeditus −(do you conceive me, sir?)

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Very well, sir.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Who cannot uti uxore pro uxore , may habere eam pro sorore .

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Absurd, absurd, absurd, and merely apostatical.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: You shall pardon me, master parson, I can prove it.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: You can prove a will, master doctor, you can prove nothing else. Does not the verse of your own canon say, Haec socianda vetant conubia, facta retractant ?

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: I grant you, but how do they retractare , master parson?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: (Oh, this was it I feared.)

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: In aeternum , sir.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: That’s false in divinity, by your favour.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: ’Tis false in humanity to say so. Is he not prorsus inutilis ad thorum ? Can he praestare fidem datam ? I would fain know.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Yes: how if he do convalere ?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: He cannot convalere , it is impossible.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: [To Morose] Nay, good sir, attend the learned men; they’ll think you neglect ’em else.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Or if he do simulare himself frigidum, odio uxoris , or so?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: I say he is adulter manifestus then.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: (They dispute it very learnedly, i’faith.)

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: And prostitutor uxoris , and this is positive.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Good sir, let me escape.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You will not do me that wrong, sir?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: And therefore, if he be manifeste frigidus , sir−

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Ay, if he be manifeste frigidus , I grant you−

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Why, that was my conclusion.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: And mine too.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Nay, hear the conclusion, sir.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Then frigiditatis causa −

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Yes, causa frigiditatis −

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, mine ears!

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: She may have libellum divortii against you.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Ay, divortii libellum she will sure have.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Good echoes, forbear.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: If you confess it.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Which I would do, sir−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I will do anything−

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: And clear myself in foro conscientiae −

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Because you want indeed−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Yet more?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Exercendi potestate .

div2.head: ACT 5 SCENE 4
div2.stage: [Enter] EPICENE, HAUGHTY, CENTAURE, MAVIS, MISTRESS OTTER, DAW, LA FOOLE.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: I will not endure it any longer. Ladies, I beseech you help me. This is such a wrong as never was offered to poor bride before. Upon her marriage-day, to have her husband conspire against her, and a couple of mercenary companions to be brought in for form’s sake, to persuade a separation! If you had blood or virtue in you, gentlemen, you would not suffer such earwigs about a husband, or scorpions to creep between man and wife−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh the variety and changes of my torment!

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Let ’em be cudgelled out of doors by our grooms.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: I’ll lend you my footman.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: We’ll have our men blanket ’em in the hall.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: As there was one at our house, madam, for peeping in at the door.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Content, i’faith.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Stay, ladies and gentlemen, you’ll hear before you proceed?

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: I’d ha’ the bridegroom blanketed too.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Begin with him first.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Yes, by my troth.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, mankind generation!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Ladies, for my sake forbear.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Yes, for Sir Dauphine’s sake.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: He shall command us.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: He is as fine a gentleman of his inches, madam, as any is about the town, and wears as good colours when he lists.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: [To Morose] Be brief, sir, and confess your infirmity, she’ll be afire to be quit of you; if she but hear that named once, you shall not entreat her to stay. She’ll fly you like one that had the marks upon him.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Ladies, I must crave all your pardons−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Silence, ladies.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: For a wrong I have done to your whole sex in marrying this fair and virtuous gentlewoman−

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Hear him, good ladies.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Being guilty of an infirmity which, before I conferred with these learned men, I thought I might have concealed−

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: But now being better informed in his conscience by them, he is to declare it and give satisfaction by asking your public forgiveness.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: I am no man, ladies.

sp.speaker: ALL
sp.p: How!

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Utterly unabled in nature, by reason of frigidity, to perform the duties or any the least office of a husband.

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Now out upon him, prodigious creature!

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: Bridegroom uncarnate.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: And would you offer it, to a young gentlewoman?

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: A lady of her longings?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Tut, a device, a device, this, it smells rankly, ladies. A mere comment of his own.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Why, if you suspect that, ladies, you may have him searched.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: As the custom is, by a jury of physicians.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Yes, faith, ’twill be brave.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh me, must I undergo that?

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: No, let women search him, madam: we can do it ourselves.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Out on me, worse!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: No, ladies, you shall not need; I’ll take him with all his faults.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Worst of all!

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Why, then ’tis no divorce, doctor, if she consent not?

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: No, if the man be frigidus , it is de parte uxoris that we grant libellum divortii in the law.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay, it is the same in theology.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Worse, worse than worst!

p.seg: Clerimont, produce your brace of knights.− What was that, master parson, you told me in errore qualitatis , e’en now? Dauphine, whisper the bride that she carry it as if she were guilty and ashamed.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Marry, sir, in errore qualitatis (which master doctor did forbear to urge) if she be found corrupta , that is, vitiated or broken up, that was pro virgine desponsa , espoused for a maid−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What then, sir?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: It doth dirimere contractum , and irritum reddere too .

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: If this be true, we are happy again, sir, once more. Here are an honourable brace of knights that shall affirm so much.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Pardon us, good Master Clerimont.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: You shall excuse us, Master Clerimont.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Nay, you must make it good now, knights, there is no remedy; I’ll eat no words for you nor no men: you know you spoke it to me?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Is this gentleman-like, sir?

p.seg: Jack Daw, he’s worse then Sir Amorous, fiercer a great deal. Sir Amorous, beware, there be ten Daws in this Clerimont.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I’ll confess it, sir.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Will you, Sir Amorous? Will you wound reputation?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: I am resolved.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: So should you be too, Jack Daw: what should keep you off? She is but a woman, and in disgrace. He’ll be glad on’t.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Will he? I thought he would ha’ been angry.

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: You will dispatch, knights; it must be done, i’faith.

p.seg: Do not tempt his patience.

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: It is true indeed, sir?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Yes, I assure you, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: What is true, gentlemen? What do you assure me?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: That we have known your bride, sir−

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: In good fashion. She was our mistress, or so−

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: Nay, you must be plain, knights, as you were to me.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Ay, the question is, if you have carnaliter or no?

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: Carnaliter ? What else, sir?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: It is enough: a plain nullity.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: I am undone, I am undone!

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, let me worship and adore you, gentlemen!

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: I am undone!

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Yes, to my hand, I thank these knights. Master parson, let me thank you otherwise.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: And ha’ they confessed?

sp.speaker: MAVIS
sp.p: Now out upon ’em, informers!

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: You see what creatures you may bestow your favours on, madams.

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: I would except against ‘em as beaten knights, wench, and not good witnesses in law.

sp.speaker: MISTRESS OTTER
sp.p: Poor gentlewoman, how she takes it!

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Be comforted, Morose, I love you the better for’t.

sp.speaker: CENTAURE
sp.p: So do I, I protest.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: But, gentlemen, you have not known her since matrimonium ?

sp.speaker: DAW
sp.p: Not today, master doctor.

sp.speaker: LA FOOLE
sp.p: No, sir, not today.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: Why, then I say, for any act before, the matrimonium is good and perfect, unless the worshipful bridegroom did precisely, before witness, demand if she were virgo ante nuptias .

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: No, that he did not, I assure you, master doctor.

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: If he cannot prove that, it is ratum conjugium , notwithstanding the premises. And they do no way impedire . And this is my sentence, this I pronounce.

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: I am of master doctor’s resolution too, sir, if you made not that demand ante nuptias .

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: O my heart! Wilt thou break? Wilt thou break? This is worst of all worst worsts! that hell could have devised! Marry a whore! and so much noise!

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Come, I see now plain confederacy in this doctor and this parson, to abuse a gentleman. You study his affliction. I pray be gone, companions. And gentlemen, I begin to suspect you for having parts with ’em. Sir, will it please you hear me?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, do not talk to me, take not from me the pleasure of dying in silence, nephew.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Sir, I must speak to you. I have been long your poor despised kinsman, and many a hard thought has strengthened you against me; but now it shall appear if either I love you or your peace, and prefer them to all the world beside. I will not be long or grievous to you, sir. If I free you of this unhappy match absolutely and instantly after all this trouble, and almost in your despair now−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: (It cannot be.)

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Sir, that you be never troubled with a murmur of it more, what shall I hope for or deserve of you?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, what thou wilt, nephew! Thou shalt deserve me and have me.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Shall I have your favour perfect to me, and love hereafter?

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: That and anything beside. Make thine own conditions. My whole estate is thine. Manage it, I will become thy ward.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Nay, sir, I will not be so unreasonable.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Will sir Dauphine be mine enemy too?

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: You know I have been long a suitor to you, uncle, that out of your estate, which is fifteen hundred a year, you would allow me but five hundred during life, and assure the rest upon me after; to which I have often by myself and friends tendered you a writing to sign, which you would never consent or incline to. If you please but to effect it now−

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Thou shalt have it, nephew. I will do it, and more.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: If I quit you not presently and for ever of this cumber, you shall have power instantly, afore all these, to revoke your act, and I will become whose slave you will give me to for ever.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Where is the writing? I will seal to it, that, or to a blank, and write thine own conditions.

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: Oh me, most unfortunate wretched gentlewoman!

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: Will Sir Dauphine do this?

sp.speaker: EPICENE
sp.p: [Weeps.] Good sir, have some compassion on me.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Oh, my nephew knows you belike; away, crocodile!

sp.speaker: HAUGHTY
sp.p: He does it not, sure, without good ground.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Here, sir.

sp.speaker: MOROSE
sp.p: Come, nephew, give me the pen. I will subscribe to anything, and seal to what thou wilt, for my deliverance. Thou art my restorer. Here, I deliver it thee as my deed. If there be a word in it lacking or writ with false orthography, I protest before− I will not take the advantage.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Then here is your release, sir: He takes off Epicene’s peruke. you have married a boy: a gentleman’s son that I have brought up this half year at my great charges, and for this composition which I have now made with you. What say you, master doctor? This is justum impedimentum , I hope, error personae ?

sp.speaker: OTTER
sp.p: Yes sir, in primo gradu .

sp.speaker: CUTBEARD
sp.p: In primo gradu .

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: I thank you, good Doctor Cutbeard and Parson Otter. He pulls off their beards and disguise. You are beholden to ’em, sir, that have taken this pains for you; and my friend, Master Truewit, who enabled ’em for the business. Now you may go in and rest, be as private as you will, sir. I’ll not trouble you till you trouble me with your funeral, which I care not how soon it come. [Exit MOROSE.] Cutbeard, I’ll make your lease good. Thank me not but with your leg, Cutbeard. And Tom Otter, your princess shall be reconciled to you.−How now, gentlemen! Do you look at me?

sp.speaker: CLERIMONT
sp.p: A boy.

sp.speaker: DAUPHINE
sp.p: Yes, Mistress Epicene.

sp.speaker: TRUEWIT
sp.p: Well, Dauphine, you have lurched your friends of the better half of the garland, by concealing this part of the plot! But much good do it thee, thou deserv’st it, lad. And Clerimont, for thy unexpected bringing in these two to confession, wear my part of it freely. Nay, sir Daw and Sir La Foole, you see the gentlewoman that has done you the favours! We are all thankful to you, and so should the womankind here, specially for lying on her, though not with her! You meant so, I am sure? But that we have stuck it upon you today in your own imagined persons, and so lately, this Amazon, the champion of the sex, should beat you now thriftily for the common slanders which ladies receive from such cuckoos as you are. You are they that, when no merit or fortune can make you hope to enjoy their bodies, will yet lie with their reputations and make their fame suffer. Away, you common moths of these and all ladies’ honours. Go, travail to make legs and faces, and come home with some new matter to be laughed at: you deserve to live in an air as corrupted as that wherewith you feed rumour. [Exeunt DAW and LA FOOLE.] Madams, you are mute upon this new metamorphosis! But here stands she that has vindicated your fames. Take heed of such insectae hereafter. And let it not trouble you that you have discovered any mysteries to this young gentleman. He is (a’most) of years, and will make a good visitant within this twelvemonth. In the meantime we’ll all undertake for his secrecy, that can speak so well of his silence. [Coming forward.] Spectators, if you like this comedy, rise cheerfully, and now Morose is gone in, clap your hands. It may be that noise will cure him, at least please him.
